transcript.content: Hello, welcome in. I'm Dr. Smith. To start, can you tell me what's been bringing you in today?

Hi, Dr. Smith. Um, honestly, the thing that finally made me come in is kind of embarrassing because it sounds small when I say it out loud, but it keeps happening at work. I’m in advertising sales, and we have these long sales strategy meetings where everyone’s supposed to just sit and listen or talk through accounts, and I know I’m supposed to stay seated, like everyone else does.

But I keep getting up. I’ll tell myself, “Just stay in the chair, it’s not that hard,” and then a few minutes later I’m up refilling my water, or I’m walking over by the printer, or I’ll pace a little like I’m checking something. Sometimes I don’t even really need water or anything from the printer. It’s more like I just can’t comfortably stay put through the whole meeting, and then afterward I’m worried people noticed or thought I was being rude or unprofessional. That’s really what pushed me to make the appointment.
Have you started or changed any new medications recently, such as antipsychotics, antiemetics, or other prescription drugs?

Um… I don’t think so. I’m trying to think if anything changed recently, because I know sometimes I forget what “recently” counts as, but no, I haven’t started anything new like that, at least not that I’m aware of.

I’m not on any new prescription that I can think of, and nobody’s put me on something like an antipsychotic or nausea medication or anything along those lines. If you mean over-the-counter stuff or supplements, I’d have to actually look at what’s in my cabinet to be totally precise, but in terms of new medications or changes, no, I don’t think there’s been anything.

Do you notice this same urge to get up and move around in other settings too—like watching a movie, sitting through a long dinner, or during quiet time at home—or does it mainly happen in meetings at work?

It’s mostly the work meetings, at least that’s where I notice it the most and where it feels like it matters the most. Like, those long sales strategy meetings are the big one—because I know I’m supposed to just sit there and look attentive, and everyone else seems able to do that, but I keep finding reasons to stand up.

I’ll get up to refill my water even if I’m not really that thirsty, or I’ll walk over near the printer like I’m checking something, or I’ll sort of pace for a minute and then come back. It’s not like I’m trying to be disruptive. It’s more that staying in the chair starts to feel really uncomfortable, and then I’m suddenly up before I’ve fully thought it through.

I guess I’m less aware of it in other places because there isn’t the same pressure to stay seated, if that makes sense. At work, it stands out because I know I shouldn’t be doing it, and then I feel self-conscious afterward.

When you feel that urge to get up during meetings, are you also experiencing worry or nervous thoughts at that moment—like fear of being judged or something going wrong—or does the urge to move happen even when you're not feeling anxious or worried about anything specific?

It’s not really like I’m sitting there thinking, “Oh no, everyone is judging me,” and then I get up because of that. The worry usually comes after, when I realize I’ve gotten up again and I’m like, great, did that look weird or unprofessional?

In the moment, it’s more physical, I guess. Like during those long sales strategy meetings, I know I’m supposed to stay in my seat, and I’ll even sort of tell myself to just stay put. But then I start feeling like I need to move, and suddenly I’m refilling my water or walking over by the printer or pacing for a second. Sometimes there isn’t even a real reason for it. I’m not necessarily anxious about something specific right then—it’s more that staying seated feels really hard, and then the self-consciousness hits afterward.

Thinking back, has this kind of difficulty sitting still and needing to move ever been a pattern for you earlier in life—like in school or previous jobs—or is this something that's really only started recently?

No, it definitely didn’t just start recently. I mean, the work meetings are where I’m noticing it most right now, but thinking back, there were signs way earlier.

I remember this being a thing before high school—like in elementary school. My teachers would write comments that I was bright, but that I rushed through things, or talked out of turn, or forgot to turn in homework. And my desk was always kind of a disaster, like stuffed with half-finished papers and random worksheets I’d started and then lost track of. I don’t know if I thought of it as “needing to move” in the same way back then, but there was definitely this pattern of being restless or not staying with things the way other kids seemed to.

So, no, it’s not new. It’s more like now I’m in a job where it’s harder to hide and there are more situations where I’m expected to sit still and look composed for a long time.
Aside from the restlessness, do you currently find it hard to stay focused on tasks, lose track of details, or forget things during your workday?

Yes, I do. It’s not constant every single minute, but it happens enough that I notice it during the workday.

The clearest example is those longer strategy meetings. I’ll start off really trying to follow the discussion, like I’m looking at the deck and listening to whoever’s talking, and then a few minutes later I realize I’ve been staring at the same slide without actually taking in what they said. It’s like my eyes are there, but my brain has wandered somewhere else, and then I’m trying to piece together the last point from context so I don’t look lost.

It also happens when I’m reading client briefs. I’ll begin with good intentions, like, okay, I need to understand the client’s goals and what they’re asking for, but then I’ll get halfway down a paragraph and realize I have no idea what I just read. So I go back and reread it, and sometimes I catch myself rereading the same section more than once because it just doesn’t stick the first time.

It’s frustrating because I’m not trying to ignore it or be careless. I’ll genuinely be trying to focus, especially if it’s important, but if it’s a longer document or a meeting that drags on, my attention just kind of slips before I realize it.
